## Biotite Feature Maps

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Make sure you have the code from the previous page"}

This is the code to [fetch genbank file from accession](biotite_entrez.qmd) from the previous page. 

Make sure you have this ready as the code on this page follows on from the last one. 
```{python}
import biotite.database.entrez as entrez
import biotite.sequence as seq
import biotite.sequence.align as align
import biotite.sequence.graphics as graphics
import biotite.sequence.io.genbank as genbank

# Define target accession for Staphylococcus cohnii strain 2-8 plasmid pSS-01
ACCESSION = "JQ041372.1"

# print a message before starting the search (as it can take some time, so this helps to show it is running)
print(f"Fetching GenBank record for accession: {ACCESSION}")

# Use entrez.fetch to find the accession, looking in the nucleotide database nuccore, and returning a gb (genbank) file
genbank_file_location = entrez.fetch(
    ACCESSION, # Accession number
    None, # Target path - we don't need this so we can set to none
    suffix="gb", # Looking for a file ending .gb (genbank file)
    db_name="nuccore", # Search the nucleotide database 
    ret_type="gb" # Return the genbank file 
)

# Read the downloaded GenBank file
genbank_file = genbank.GenBankFile.read(genbank_file_location)

# Open and print the entire raw GenBank file content
# print(f"--- Full GenBank File Content for {ACCESSION} ---")
# print(genbank_file)
```

:::

## Genome Feature Map & Explanations

Now we have our genbank file with our DNA sequence and the locations of all of our genes, we can combine `biotite` with `matplotlib` to generate a map of all of the genes. 

### Step 1: Extracting Organism Metadata
Our genbank file has a field called `"SOURCE"` which contains some useful information about the organism. 

```{python}
# Use source to extract organism information
source = genbank_file.get_fields("SOURCE")
print(source)
```

From here we can see that there is a dictionary called `subfields` with a key `"ORGANISM"` - this is a list of the entire taxonomy. 

`"ORGANISM": ['Staphylococcus cohnii', 'Bacteria; Bacillati; Bacillota; Bacilli; Caryophanales;', 'Staphylococcaceae; Staphylococcus; Staphylococcus cohnii species', 'complex.']`

To get the species name, we can use the key `"ORGANISM"` to get the above list, and extract the first entry (species) by using the index `[0]`. 
```{python}
species = source[0].subfields["ORGANISM"][0]
print(f"Target Species: {species}")
```

### Step 2: Filtering Coding Sequences (CDS) & Genes
GenBank files contain many annotation types (such as `CDS`, `gene`, `tRNA`, `rRNA`). We can filter specifically for gene features while excluding RNA genes to focus purely on protein-coding regions, and use this to build a map of the genes. 

```{python}
# Extract the annotations using the genbank get_annotation feature
annotation = genbank.get_annotation(
     #include only will only include "gene" and not "CDS", "tRNA" etc.
    genbank_file, include_only=["gene"] 
)

# Select genes only and filter out tRNAs and rRNAs if present
# make an empty list
gene_features = []
# use a for loop to go through each feature in the annotation 
for feature in annotation: 
    # use if/else to check they are genes 
    # tRNAs and rRNAs will appear as genes as well
    # Can use an if statement to remove them
    if (
        feature.key == "gene" # Check it is a gene 
        and "trn" not in str(feature) # don't include tRNAs
        and "rrn" not in str(feature) # don't include rRNAs
        ):
        # add to the list 
        gene_features.append(feature) 
```

### Step 3: Plotting the Linear Feature Map
Finally, we set up a Matplotlib figure axis and call `graphics.plot_feature_map()` to render the positions of the extracted genes along the plasmid sequence.

Once you have the plot - look up the gene names. How many antimicrobial resistance genes are there? What are the other elements? 

```{python}
# Import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a figure with the dimensions 15x2 
# This will be an empty plot that biotite can add to 
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 2))

# Use biotite plot_feature_map function to plot the map with the gene locations
graphics.plot_feature_map(
    plt.gca(), #gca() is get current axes - will get the figure we made above 
    seq.Annotation(gene_features), # Add the chosen annotations
    multi_line=False, # This is a small plasmid so we want it on one line
    show_line_position=True # This will show the locations (DNA base pair numbers) at the bottom 
)

# Adding a title for the map
plt.title(
    f"Genome map - {species} ({ACCESSION})"
)

# Show the plot
plt.show()
```
